To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a 10 percent increase in life expectancy is associated with a 0.7 percentage point increase in the probability of attending high school and a 2.5 percentage point increase in high-school graduation rates.
a large increase in life expectancy during the second half in the 20th Century was associated with a significant rise in human capital formation in developed countries.
a 10-year increase in life expectancy is associated with a 1.7-year increase in years of schooling, and that the effect is mainly driven by the reduction in pneumonia mortality.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the epidemiological transition affected the formation of human and physical capital, and how the latter two factors in turn affected economic growth.
how the epidemiological transition has affected the human capital formation process.
the role of health as a driver of economic development.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
life expectancy is an important determinant of human capital accumulation and that improvements in childhood health are the main reason behind this result.

a one-year increase in life expectancy increases human capital by 0.15 years, and this increase is driven by the decline of mortality from infectious diseases, especially pneumonia, during the second half.
the rise in human capital over the second half of 20th century is a direct outcome of the epidemiological transition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the rise in mortality in childhood is a key factor behind the rise in human capital in the 20th-century developed world.
the rise in the average level of human capital is a major factor explaining the growth in per capita income over the last century.

the rise in human capital is the result of a combination of the following three factors: (i) a positive shock in mortality due to the medical breakthroughs, (ii) the subsequent rise in life expectancy, and (iii) the positive effect of life expectancy on human capital.
The main takeaway from our work is that
human capital formation in developed countries is highly sensitive to health shocks.
human capital accumulation is a dynamic process that is sensitive to changes in life expectancy.

, in the context of the international epidemiological transitions, a positive shock to life expectancies has been a major contributor to the increase in human wealth in the second half of 20th century.
